# I want [**these**]{.contentchip} sentences with [**this**]{.formatchip} layout

::: {.col .amberborder}
![](images/handwriting-practice-pokemon.png){fig-align="center" height="600"}
:::

::: {.col .blueborder}

::: {.notes}
Here's the problem with asking a model for a document.

I didn't want *a* handwriting sheet. I wanted **these words** in **this layout**.

Those are two different things — and when I ask for the finished document, I've
asked the model to generate both of them at the same time.
:::

{{< center >}}

# [Content]{.contentchip} entangled with [Format]{.formatchip}

{{< include svg/entanglement-1.qmd >}}

::: {.notes}
What actually happened across those eight rounds?

Every time I re-prompted, I wasn't changing the thing I didn't like. I was
rolling the dice on the entire document again.

The model isn't editing a document. It's generating another document.

Don't say "LLMs are bad at formatting" — too easy to rebut. The argument is
that generation is probabilistic and rendering is deterministic.

Optional heading, if "entangled" feels like a word the audience has to accept
before the figure can work: **Every fix is a new document.** That is the actual
claim, and it needs no metaphor.
:::

# Quarto disentangles [Content]{.contentchip .fragment .custom .turnsred data-fragment-index="3"} and [Format]{.formatchip}

{{< include svg/entanglement-2.qmd >}}

::: {.notes}
Define Quarto out loud here, about eight seconds: it's a plain-text
document — markdown with code in it — and `quarto render` turns it into a PDF,
or a website, or these slides.

The point isn't that the .qmd is prettier. It's that the weaving moved somewhere
I can reach, and reaching it took one step instead of eight.

Optional heading: **The weaving moves to render time.** Slightly more concrete
than "disentangles," and it sets up the next slide, which shows the seam.
:::

# [One `.qmd`, one folder of CSVs]{.center}

:::: {.col width="58%"}
[**`handwriting-practice.qmd`**]{.qmdblue .font120}

(written by Claude Code)

<br>

::: {.font70}
````{.markdown}
---
params:
  data_file: "data/sentences-mario.csv"
format: pdf
---

```{{r}}
sentences <- read.csv(params$data_file)$sentence
for (s in sentences) {
  cat(sprintf("\\practiceblock{%s}\n\n", s))
}
```
````
:::
::::

:::: {.col width="42%"}
[**`sentences-minecraft.csv`**]{.amber .font120}

(written by Me)

<br>

:::{.font70}
|sentence |
|-----|
|Minecraft is a popular building game.|
|Players mine for resources underground.|
|You can build almost anything you want.|
|Creepers are sneaky and dangerous enemies.|
|Diamonds are the best ore to find.|
|Players must survive through the first night.|
|The Nether is a hot and scary place.|
:::

::::

::: {.notes}
Two files. The model wrote the left one, once. It has never seen the right one.

**Click 1 — the parameters.** The sentences aren't in the document. They're in a
file, and which file is an argument. That's what "the content has an address"
actually looks like on disk.

**Click 2 — the elision.** Those forty lines are TikZ: line heights, baselines,
the grey trace text the kid writes over. That is the format. I wrote it once and
I have not opened it since.

**Click 3 — the read.** One line. That's where the two halves meet, and it
happens at render, not in the model.

And because the file is parameterized, it isn't one worksheet — it's a worksheet
*generator*. A four-line loop renders every CSV in that folder into its own PDF.
Pokemon, minecraft, mario: same source.

Don't show `render.R`. Say "four lines" and move on; the loop is not the idea.

⚠️ Replace the CSV rows and the header with the real ones. This is the one slide
in the deck whose whole job is being a real file, so it must not stay a mock-up.

⚠️ Decide against the closing *change one word* slide (`format: pdf` →
`format: html`). Both slides change one thing in the YAML. Different claims —
many topics here, many formats there — but if they read as the same trick, the
second one deflates. Pick which gets the emphasis.
:::

**~3,000 lines** of markdown and code — and not one file over a few hundred.

The data loads at render:

[`library(vehicletrends)`]{.font140 .blue}

I typed none of the numbers.
:::

::: {.notes}
This isn't a 3,000-line dashboard. It's 15 small documents.

That distinction matters enormously once an agent is working on it — and it's
the same distinction as the handwriting sheet, just at a bigger scale.

The agent writes the `.qmd`. The data lives in a package the pages load at
render.

Plant `library(vehicletrends)` deliberately — you are coming back to this exact
line in the correctness section, and the callback only works if they saw it
land here.
:::

---

## It's not an application. It's a document.

::: {.col}
[**Shiny**]{.red}

- a UI
- a server function
- a reactive graph
- a process that has to be running

You maintain an **application**.
:::

::: {.col}
[**Quarto**]{.blue}

- markdown
- a chunk that returns a widget

You maintain a **document**.
:::

[No UI. No server. Real compute over data too big for a browser is still Shiny's job.]{.font120}

::: {.notes}
This isn't an application. It's a document.

Not an anti-Shiny argument: real server-side compute over data too big for a
browser is exactly Shiny's job. Most dashboards aren't that.

This slide is early on purpose. This room has been silently asking "why isn't
this Shiny?" since the montage, and you cannot argue cost and correctness to
people who are still stuck on that question. Answer it, then move.
:::

<img src="images/fig-tokens.png" width=100%>

::: {.notes}
The agent pays for every character.

And it compounds over turns: about 81,000 tokens versus about 11,000 after ten
edits. The ratio never moves — the gap does.

The sharper version of the whole cost argument, worth saying out loud right
here: **it is not that markdown is smaller — it is that you stop paying for the
parts you did not change.** Character count is the proxy; regeneration is the
mechanism.
:::

# [Quarto is checkable twice]{.center}

<br>

::: {.col .fragment}
## [**By machine**]{.darkgreen}

### `quarto render` is a compile step

<pre class="specimen errcard">
<span class="sp-dim">Quitting from index.qmd:12-30 [africa-map]</span>
<span class="sp-err">Error:</span>
<span class="sp-err">! all(funding$name %in% africa$name) is not TRUE</span>
<span>Execution halted</span>
</pre>

:::

::: {.col .fragment}
## [**By human**]{.darkgreen}

### Plain text means the edit is a **diff**

<pre class="specimen diffcard">
<span>  ## EV Sales</span>
<span> </span>
<span>  Sales of **electric vehicles** grew 20% in 2025,</span>
<span class="sp-del">- reaching <span class="w">over</span> _20 million_ sales globally.</span>
<span class="sp-add">+ reaching <span class="w">nearly</span> _20 million_ sales globally.</span>
</pre>

:::

::: {.notes}
By machine: `quarto render` is a compile step, and an assertion can
fail the build.

By human: plain text means the edit is a diff. Review scales with the change,
not with the document.
:::

---

## [HTML is good, but it can't tell you if it's broken]{.center}

::: {.col .fragment}
[**HTML** - _manual_ numbers]{.red}

::: {.font140}
<pre class="specimen diffcard compact">
<span>  &lt;!DOCTYPE html&gt;</span>
<span>  &lt;html lang="en"&gt;</span>
<span>  &lt;head&gt;</span>
<span>  &lt;meta charset="utf-8"&gt;</span>
<span>  &lt;title&gt;EV Sales&lt;/title&gt;</span>
<span>  &lt;style&gt;</span>
<span>  body { font-family: Georgia, serif;</span>
<span>         max-width: 40em; margin: 3em auto; }</span>
<span>  h2 { font-size: 1.6em; }</span>
<span>  &lt;/style&gt;</span>
<span>  &lt;/head&gt;</span>
<span>  &lt;body&gt;</span>
<span>  &lt;h2&gt;EV Sales&lt;/h2&gt;</span>
<span>  &lt;p&gt;Sales of &lt;strong&gt;electric vehicles&lt;/strong&gt; grew</span>
<span class="sp-del">- 20% in 2025, reaching over &lt;em&gt;<span class="w">18 million</span>&lt;/em&gt;</span>
<span class="sp-add">+ 20% in 2025, reaching over &lt;em&gt;<span class="w">20 million</span>&lt;/em&gt;</span>
<span>  sales globally.&lt;/p&gt;</span>
<span>  &lt;/body&gt;</span>
<span>  &lt;/html&gt;</span>
</pre>
:::

:::

::: {.col .fragment}
[**`.qmd`** - _computed_ numbers]{.blue}

::: {.font140}
<pre class="specimen diffcard compact">
<span>  ## EV Sales</span>
<span> </span>
<span>  Sales of **electric vehicles** grew</span>
<span>  20% in 2025, reaching over</span>
<span class="sp-del">- _<span class="w">20 million</span>_ sales globally.</span>
<span class="sp-add">+ _<span class="w">&#96;r ev_sales&#96; million</span>_ sales globally.</span>
</pre>
:::

:::

::: {.notes}
Why not just ask for HTML? Agents are very good at it.

Because malformed HTML still renders as *something*, so the agent can't tell
whether it succeeded.

Left: nineteen lines, and the changed row has somewhere to hide. Right: compute
it once and never re-type it.
:::

## Interactivity lives in the browser

::: {.col width="40%"}
*"But I need users to filter it."*

::: {.font45}
```r
depreciation |>
  filter(powertrain == "Gasoline") |>
  group_by(vehicle_type) |>
  e_charts(age_years) |>
  e_line(rr_smooth) |>
  e_legend()
```
:::

[Click a category in the legend →]{.font110}

[No input. No server. No reactive.]{.font110 .blue}

[I just put the widget in the document.]{.font120}
:::

::: {.col width="60%"}
```{r}
smooth_group <- function(df) {
  fit <- loess(rr ~ age_years, data = df, span = 0.5)
  df$rr_smooth <- predict(fit)
  df
}

depreciation |>
  filter(powertrain == "Gasoline", quantile == 50) |>
  mutate(age_years = age_bin / 12) |>
  group_by(vehicle_type) |>
  group_modify(~ smooth_group(.x)) |>
  e_charts(age_years, height = "460px") |>
  e_line(rr_smooth, symbol = "none", smooth = FALSE) |>
  e_legend(bottom = 0, textStyle = list(fontSize = 18)) |>
  e_tooltip(trigger = "axis") |>
  e_y_axis(name = "Retention rate", nameLocation = "middle", nameGap = 50) |>
  e_x_axis(name = "Age (years)") |>
  e_grid(left = 90, right = 40, top = 30, bottom = 90)
```
:::

::: {.notes}
The point is not "Quarto supports JavaScript."

The point is that I can put an interactive widget in a document without building
the application around it.

Click a category in the legend — live. No input, no server, no reactive.
:::

## Or drop a whole Shiny app in the page

Two pages on the site **are** Shiny apps — compiled to WebAssembly, running in
the reader's browser:

````markdown

#| viewerHeight: 800
```
````

[Same move. The hard thing goes in a box, and the page just says where.]{.font120}

Same move. The hard thing goes in a box, and the page just says where.

Two pages on the site are Shiny apps compiled to WebAssembly, running in the
reader's browser.

---

## It's just static files

Everything here runs in the browser, and the whole site is files — **hosted for free.**

- charts → ECharts (JS), rendered client-side
- the map → PMTiles on a CDN, instant
- the Shiny app → **Shinylive**, compiled to WebAssembly. No server.

A GitHub Action re-renders and republishes it **every Sunday at 5am.** Nothing is
cached, so nothing goes stale.

[No server to run. No server to secure. No server to pay for.]{.font120}

::: {.notes}
Say "static files," not "serverless" — serverless drags in Lambda and edge
functions and backends. This is simpler than that.

At the end of the day it's a folder of files a browser can read. So I can host
it for free.

If you kept the correctness-at-scale slide, the Sunday re-render is already
spent. Drop that sentence here and let this slide be purely about hosting.
:::

## Where this gets annoying

- agents invent chunk options that don't exist — `quarto render` catches it, but only if you make them run it
- Quarto's errors point at the **rendered** line, not always the line you wrote
- a big render loop is slow; cache it or the agent will wait, and so will you
- models still write 2023-era Quarto — expect `output:` where you wanted `format:`

[None of these are fatal. All of them are cheaper than re-prompting a PDF.]{.font120}

::: {.notes}
NEW SLIDE — RECOMMENDED. Edit the four bullets down to whatever actually bit
you; the specific gripes matter less than the fact that you have some.

This buys credibility with the skeptic in row three, and it makes the next
slide read as mitigation rather than boilerplate. A talk that admits nothing
gets argued with in the hallway.

Keep it fast — twenty seconds, no dwelling. The last line is the whole point of
the slide.
:::

---

## Make this work Monday

1. Put *"always run `quarto render` before finishing"* in your `CLAUDE.md`
2. Have the agent work on a branch, so edits arrive as diffs
3. Keep data in files the `.qmd` reads — never in the prompt

::: {.notes}
Three things you can do Monday.

Read them fast. If you added the caveats slide before this one, these three now
read as mitigations, which is a better register than advice.
:::
